newsitem.title: USA: Cunanan's death brings joy to South Beach.
newsitem.headline: Cunanan's death brings joy to South Beach.

text.p: They were the words the night-crawling denizens of South Beach most wanted to hear.
"The reign of terror brought upon us by Andrew Cunanan is over," Miami Beach Police Chief Richard Barreto announced shortly before dawn on Thursday.
Word of the alleged serial killer's death raced through the all-night diners, bars and nightclubs of glitzy South Beach, where the drag shows were just ending.

Some residents kept an all-night vigil at television sets, waiting for police confirmation that Cunanan, accused of the murders of Italian fashion designer Gianni Versace and four other men, had died of a gunshot wound aboard a houseboat just three miles (4.8 km) to the north.
"Thank God, thank God," cried Edgar Utroska, clutching his purse outside Hombre, a gay bar. "I was so afraid because in my mind, I always thought, 'He's in Miami Beach, he's in Miami Beach.'"

Cunanan's possible presence in South Beach had cast a giant shadow over the gay club scene since Versace's slaying on the steps of his Ocean Drive mansion on July 15. Attendance dropped at drag shows in the days after the killing. Gay men would not leave their homes alone at night, even pairing up to walk their dogs.

Cunanan, a gay prostitute who befriended wealthy older men, was believed to have lived in the bohemian Art Deco district for up to two months before the killing. South Beach is a mecca for gay tourists and has a resident homosexual population of some 12,000, gay community leaders said.
Utroska, a drag queen clad in a shimmering silver halter top, bell bottoms and high heels, said Versace was his fashion icon as he dressed for shows in the local clubs.

"My big inspiration was Versace. I really feel so sad about him," he said. "I'm doing drag and I'm always looking at the magazines, always looking at his style and saying 'Oh, I love this dress.' Versace always."
"Life can get back to some semblance of normal here," said Patric Chemaly, 27, a rollerblading medical student who said he had learned of Cunanan's death on the Internet.
"I think people were afraid to go out. They were always wondering if the trick they took home was Andrew," he said. "I think it's really taught people you have to be careful who you meet."
But some South Beach residents said Cunanan's death left too many unanswered questions about Versace and the alleged cross-country killing spree.

"I feel that if he would have gotten arrested it would have been a lot better, because he would have paid back a little for what he did," said David Guerra, 17. "Now he's dead and it's over. I would like to know what he got out of killing all those people."
